_doc: HMTc Category 8 (Water and Water-Based Products) compiler config. Method v2.0, government-limit-only. This is the most comprehensively regulated category in the HMTc taxonomy: nine of the eleven panel cells carry a number on every row (eight direct sovereign maxima plus a disclosed read-across on the mineral-water row, where aluminium is the one cell no government sets for natural mineral water; nine direct sovereign maxima on the other three rows), because two whole instrument families reach the product form — national drinking-water regulations (US EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulations as incorporated by FDA, EU Directive 2020/2184, Health Canada GDWQ, NHMRC ADWG, California SWRCB Title 22, WHO GDWQ) and the packaged-water lines of national food-contaminant schedules (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, India FSSAI 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Chile Decreto 977/1996, Fiji FSR 2009). Every number is a named register id; none is occurrence-derived. Two cells carry no number on any row and are handled honestly rather than invented: tin, for which no government sets a water maximum and for which the only near-neighbour (canned-beverage tinplate migration at 100 mg/kg) is four orders of magnitude out of range, is a CONTROL; methylmercury, which no government regulates in water and which is bounded by identity under the published total-mercury ceiling, is NOT-MATERIAL on the speciation-bounded basis class. Two deliberate departures from HMTc defaults are documented in _category.method_note and in the affected cells' substantiation: total chromium is published as a FIRM limit rather than a screen (the drinking-water instruments regulate the total because the species interconvert in water, and Health Canada says so in terms), and the credible-regulator set is widened to the authorities that actually publish a packaged-water metals line so the stricter-unselected audit scans the complete instrument pool. Allowed provenance tags: regulatory-alignment, read-across, not-material, control, ratchet. STAFF / HMTc content, not public wiki (CLAUDE.md Part 19 firewall).

_category.name: Water and Water-Based Products
_category.anchor: strictest applicable sovereign drinking-water or packaged-water maximum, per litre of finished product as consumed, with the natural-mineral-water product-form split preserved as the governments write it
_category.basis_family: dietary as-consumed, per litre of finished packaged water (µg/L, numerically interchangeable with µg/kg at unit density)
_category.method_label: HMTc Method v2.0 (government-limit default; strictest applicable sovereign maximum for the exact packaged-water form in its native per-litre as-consumed basis, disclosed read-across where the exact cell is unregulated, control where no defensible sovereign number exists; never occurrence-derived)
_category.method_note: Two applicability rules govern every row in this category and are applied uniformly. (1) THE PACKAGED-WATER BRIDGE. A national drinking-water maximum is treated as directly applicable to a packaged-water row because the product is the same substance assessed in the same basis (µg per litre of water as consumed), and because the two largest jurisdictions write that bridge into their own packaged-water rules: the FDA bottled-water standard of quality incorporates the EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulation maximum contaminant levels by reference at 21 CFR 165.110(b)(4)(iii), and the scope of EU Directive 2020/2184 expressly reaches water put into bottles or containers. The bridge is disclosed, not silent, and it is never applied where the instrument itself carves the product form out. (2) THE NATURAL-MINERAL-WATER CARVE-OUT. Directive 2020/2184 excludes natural mineral waters recognised under Directive 2009/54/EC, so no Drinking Water Directive value is used on the mineral-water row; and FDA exempts mineral water from its aesthetically based (secondary) allowable levels, which is why the mineral-water aluminium cell is a disclosed read-across rather than a direct government limit. Where the instruments write a product-form split, the split is preserved: mineral-water total chromium is 50 µg/L (Hong Kong Cap 132V natural-mineral-waters line, matched by Health Canada, WHO and California) while other packaged drinking water is 25 µg/L (Directive Annex I Part B). UNIT BASIS. Every value is expressed per litre of finished packaged product as consumed. Instruments stating mg/kg (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011) and instruments stating mg/L are compared at face value because the density of potable water is within 0.3 per cent of 1 kg/L across the packaging and storage range, so µg/kg and µg/L are the same number to well inside analytical uncertainty. No reconstitution or dilution conversion is applied anywhere in this category; the 8:1 powder-to-liquid conversion is confined to infant formula and is expressly not used on the infant nursery-water row. TOTAL CHROMIUM IS FIRM, NOT A SCREEN. In a food matrix total chromium is dominated by nutritionally benign Cr(III) and is a poor proxy for the health-relevant species, which is why HMTc normally records it as a screen. Water is the documented exception: the drinking-water instruments regulate total chromium precisely because the two species interconvert in aqueous media, and the Health Canada entry states that the maximum acceptable concentration protects against chromium(VI) effects and is established for total chromium. Hexavalent chromium is additionally published as its own cell, so the species control is not displaced by the total. NON-HEALTH-BASED AND FUTURE-DATED ANCHORS ARE LABELLED. Aluminium at 200 µg/L is an EU Annex I Part C indicator parameter, an FDA secondary (aesthetic) allowable level and an NHMRC aesthetic guideline, and is presented as such rather than as a toxicological line. The EU lead (5 µg/L) and total-chromium (25 µg/L) parametric values are the Directive's end-state values, which member states must meet by 12 January 2036 and below which transitional values of 10 and 50 µg/L apply until then; HMTc adopts the end-state values now, so those cells are stricter than currently-enforced EU practice, which is disclosed rather than presented as current EU law. For lead the number is independently compelled by the in-force FDA allowable level of 5 µg/L.
_category.credible_note: Category 8 is governed by two instrument families: national drinking-water regulations and the packaged-water lines of national food-contaminant schedules. The default credible set (EU, UK, Codex, international, US, AU-NZ, CA, HK) omits most of the authorities that actually publish a packaged-water metals line, which would leave the stricter-unselected audit scanning only a fraction of the applicable pool and would risk exactly the missed-stricter-anchor failure the audit exists to catch. The set is therefore widened to every jurisdiction in the register that publishes a drinking-water or packaged-water maximum for a panel analyte: AU (NHMRC Australian Drinking Water Guidelines), US-CA (California State Water Resources Control Board Title 22 section 64431 inorganic-chemical MCLs, the only enforceable hexavalent-chromium drinking-water maximum anywhere in the register), WHO (Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality), IL, IN, VN, GSO, CO, CL and FJ. Admission to the scan pool is not endorsement and does not by itself make a value binding: a row binds only where it is applicable to the exact product form AND is the strictest such value, and the widening is what makes the audit's silence meaningful. WHO guideline values are advisory rather than national law (the register records this on the rows themselves) and are carried for corroboration and audit completeness; no published value in this category rests on a WHO guideline value as its binding source. California is a sub-national government and its selection on the hexavalent-chromium cell is disclosed as such in that cell's substantiation.

bottled-drinking-water.name: Bottled drinking water (purified, spring, artesian)
bottled-drinking-water.native_basis_label: as consumed, per litre of finished bottled water (µg/L; numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
bottled-drinking-water.scope_note: This row is packaged water as placed on the market and assessed per litre as consumed. It is governed by the packaged-water bridge stated in the category method note: national drinking-water maxima apply because the product is the same substance in the same basis, and because FDA incorporates the EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulation MCLs into the bottled-water standard of quality at 21 CFR 165.110(b)(4)(iii) while the scope of EU Directive 2020/2184 expressly reaches water put into bottles or containers. In scope: purified, distilled, deionised, reverse-osmosis, spring, artesian and well water sold packaged for drinking, unflavoured and unsweetened, in any container. Out of scope: natural mineral water, which is a legally distinct product form with its own row and its own instrument (EU Directive 2009/54/EC and Commission Directive 2003/40/EC; the Hong Kong Cap 132V line for this row reads 'bottled or packaged drinking waters, OTHER THAN natural mineral waters'); unflavoured carbonated water, which has its own row; and any flavoured, sweetened, mineral-fortified, vitamin-added or functional water, which routes to HMTc Category 5 (Beverages) by the Category 8 boundary rule because flavouring changes both the matrix and the regulatory treatment. Water sold for formula preparation routes to the infant nursery-water row.
bottled-drinking-water.cross_reference: Flavoured, sweetened or functional waters route to HMTc Category 5 (Beverages). Natural mineral water is the mineral-water row of this category.

bottled-drinking-water.basis_guard_note: Every named anchor must be a dietary per-litre / as-consumed water or food-schedule basis. The guard rejects dry-weight, dehydrated, migration/leachate, article material-content and feed bases outright, so a dry-commodity maximum level or a food-contact migration limit can never anchor a per-litre water cell. It admits mg/kg-expressed food-schedule rows (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011) because potable water density is within 0.3 per cent of 1 kg/L, so µg/kg and µg/L are the same number to well inside analytical uncertainty; that is a stated identity, not a silent conversion.

Pb.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum for packaged drinking water (EU Drinking Water Directive Annex I Part B end-state value; matched by FDA 21 CFR 165.110, Health Canada and NHMRC)
Pb.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Pb.substantiation: Lead at 5 µg/L is the strictest applicable sovereign maximum and it is corroborated four ways: the EU Drinking Water Directive Annex I Part B parametric value, the FDA bottled-water allowable level at 21 CFR 165.110 (0.005 mg/L), the Health Canada maximum acceptable concentration and the NHMRC health-based guideline value. The Directive's 5 µg/L is its end-state value, which member states must meet by 12 January 2036 and below which the transitional value of 10 µg/L applies until then; HMTc adopts the end-state value now, so this cell is stricter than currently-enforced EU practice, but the FDA value of 5 µg/L is in force today and is independently sufficient to compel the number. The looser 10 µg/L values (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, the WHO provisional guideline value, and the Codex/mineral-water family) are named in the candidate set and are not selected because the method takes the strictest applicable value.

Cd.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum (NHMRC Australian Drinking Water Guidelines health-based guideline value)
Cd.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Cd.substantiation: Cadmium at 2 µg/L is the NHMRC Australian Drinking Water Guidelines health-based guideline value (0.002 mg/L), the strictest cadmium maximum any government sets for water. It is applied under the packaged-water bridge stated in the category method note: the product is the same substance in the same per-litre as-consumed basis, and the guideline carries no packaged-product carve-out. The next tier is 3 µg/L (WHO, Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013), then 5 µg/L (EU Drinking Water Directive, FDA 21 CFR 165.110, EPA MCL, California), then 7 µg/L (Health Canada). All are named in the candidate set; none is selected because 2 µg/L is applicable and stricter.

tAs.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum; unanimous at 10 µg/L across the applicable instrument pool
tAs.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
tAs.substantiation: Total arsenic at 10 µg/L is unanimous across every applicable instrument in the pool: EU Drinking Water Directive, FDA 21 CFR 165.110, the EPA MCL adopted into the bottled-water standard of quality by reference, California, Health Canada, NHMRC, Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011 and the WHO provisional guideline value. There is no stricter sovereign total-arsenic value for water anywhere in the register. Total arsenic is published as its own cell and is not satisfied by the inorganic-arsenic cell.

iAs.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum for the exact product form (Israel FCS 2016 row 16.1, bottled drinking water and mineral water)
iAs.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
iAs.substantiation: Inorganic arsenic at 6 µg/L is the Israel FCS 2016 maximum level for the exact product form ('Bottled drinking water and mineral water', source row 16.1, 0.006 mg/kg), the strictest sovereign inorganic-arsenic maximum for packaged water in the register. The alternatives are the US EPA drinking-water MCL recorded as inorganic arsenic at 10 µg/L and the Chilean Decreto 977/1996 Article 160 value of 10 µg/L for mineral and packaged drinking waters; both are named and neither is selected because 6 µg/L is applicable and stricter. The species cell is retained separately from total arsenic even though arsenic in potable water is effectively all inorganic, because the HMTc panel never allows a species to satisfy a total: a lot must clear both 10 µg/L total arsenic and 6 µg/L inorganic arsenic.

tHg.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum (EU Drinking Water Directive Annex I Part B; matched by NHMRC, Health Canada and Israel FCS 2016)
tHg.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
tHg.substantiation: Total mercury at 1 µg/L is the strictest applicable sovereign maximum, set independently by the EU Drinking Water Directive Annex I Part B, the NHMRC health-based guideline, the Health Canada maximum acceptable concentration (which the source table states applies to all forms of mercury) and the Israel FCS 2016 packaged-water line. The FDA bottled-water allowable level and the California MCL are 2 µg/L and the Vietnamese bottled-water value is 6 µg/L; all are named and none is selected. Total mercury is published as a total and is never satisfied by a methylmercury or inorganic-mercury result.

not_material.rationale: Mercury in sealed packaged drinking water is present essentially as inorganic Hg(II). Methylation is a microbial process requiring anaerobic sulfate- or iron-reducing activity in sediment or biota; it does not occur in a treated, filtered, disinfected and sealed packaged-water matrix, and there is no aquatic food chain in the product to bioaccumulate methylmercury. Methylmercury is in any event a component of total mercury, so it is bounded by identity at the published total-mercury ceiling of 1 µg/L. No separate methylmercury ceiling is published.
not_material.reference_method: Methylmercury is not separately quantified as a routine cell. Total mercury is measured on every certification lot by cold-vapour atomic fluorescence or ICP-MS against the published total-mercury ceiling. Where a lot result reaches or exceeds half the total-mercury ceiling, speciation by GC-ICP-MS or HPLC-ICP-MS is run as a reflex and the source water is investigated; a detectable methyl fraction is an immediate non-conformance regardless of the total-mercury result.
not_material.regulatory_basis: No jurisdiction sets a methylmercury maximum for drinking water, bottled water or natural mineral water. Every drinking-water and packaged-water instrument in the pool regulates mercury as total mercury with no methyl line, and Hong Kong Cap 132V regulates the packaged-drinking-water mercury cell as INORGANIC mercury (0.006 mg/kg, hk_cap132v_ihg_bottled-or-packaged-drinking-waters-other-than-natural_6), which is direct sovereign confirmation that the regulated mercury species in packaged water is the inorganic one. The only methylmercury maxima anywhere in the register are fish and aquatic-animal limits (for example fda_cpg540600_mehg_fish_1000), which govern a bioaccumulating tissue matrix and have no application to water.
not_material.jurisdictions_checked: EU Directive 2020/2184 Annex I; EU Commission Directive 2003/40/EC (natural mineral waters); US EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulations; US FDA 21 CFR 165.110; California SWRCB Title 22 s.64431; Health Canada Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality (2025 summary tables); NHMRC Australian Drinking Water Guidelines; WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality; Hong Kong Cap 132V Part 2; Israel FCS 2016; India FSSAI 2016; Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011; GSO 193/2021; Colombia Res 4506/2013; Chile Decreto 977/1996; Fiji FSR 2009.

Ni.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum (EU Drinking Water Directive Annex I Part B; matched by NHMRC)
Ni.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Ni.substantiation: Nickel at 20 µg/L is the EU Drinking Water Directive Annex I Part B parametric value, matched exactly by the NHMRC health-based guideline and by the Hong Kong Cap 132V natural-mineral-waters line. The looser candidates are Hong Kong's 70 µg/L for other packaged drinking waters, the WHO guideline value of 70 µg/L, and 100 µg/L from FDA 21 CFR 165.110 and California; all are named and none is selected. The FDA and California nickel values descend from an EPA nickel MCL that was remanded in 1995, which is a further reason not to treat 100 µg/L as the operative ceiling when a current statutory value of 20 µg/L is applicable.

control.rationale: No sovereign sets a tin maximum for drinking water, bottled water or natural mineral water. The drinking-water instrument family carries no tin parameter at all (EU Directive 2020/2184 Annex I Parts B and C; US EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulations; US FDA 21 CFR 165.110 standards of quality; Health Canada; NHMRC; WHO), and none of the national food-schedule packaged-water lines (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, India FSSAI 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Chile Decreto 977/1996, Fiji FSR 2009) carries a tin entry for water. A read-across is not supportable: the nearest sovereign tin maxima are the canned-food and canned-beverage maximum levels, which exist to bound dissolution of tin from a tinplate container wall into an acidic canned matrix, and the canned-beverage value (100 mg/kg inorganic tin) sits roughly four orders of magnitude above anything a packaged water can plausibly contain, so importing it would publish a ceiling that functions as no limit at all. The dominant packaging for this category (PET, HDPE, glass, aluminium) contains no tin. Still bottled water is occasionally presented in aluminium or tin-free steel cans, neither of which is a tin source. Tin therefore remains a mandatory control cell; no number is invented.
control.reference_method: Tin by ICP-MS on the finished packaged product in its native per-litre as-consumed basis, on every certification lot, reported against the method limit of quantification rather than a ceiling. Any quantifiable tin result triggers investigation of the container, closure and liner, the filling line and the source water, and lot release is withheld pending root-cause identification and a clean re-test. Where the product is presented in a tinplate or tin-coated container, the EU canned-beverage inorganic-tin maximum level recorded as the companion instrument applies as a regulatory hard stop in addition to this control.

Al.label: strictest applicable sovereign value; an indicator / secondary / aesthetic parameter, disclosed as such
Al.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Al.substantiation: Aluminium at 200 µg/L is the strictest applicable sovereign value and is disclosed here as a non-health-based parameter rather than a toxicological line: it is an Annex I Part C INDICATOR parameter in the EU Drinking Water Directive, a SECONDARY (aesthetically based) allowable level at FDA 21 CFR 165.110, and an AESTHETIC guideline for acid-soluble aluminium in the NHMRC guidelines. The health-based alternatives are far looser (Health Canada's maximum acceptable concentration of 2900 µg/L; California's MCL of 1000 µg/L), so adopting 200 µg/L is the strictest applicable treatment and is materially protective. Its aesthetic derivation is stated rather than concealed because the label of the parameter, not only its number, is part of the provenance.

Cr.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum (EU Drinking Water Directive Annex I Part B end-state value)
Cr.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Cr.substantiation: Total chromium at 25 µg/L is the EU Drinking Water Directive Annex I Part B parametric value, the strictest applicable sovereign maximum; it is the Directive's end-state value, to be met by 12 January 2036, with a transitional value of 50 µg/L in force until then. The 50 µg/L tier (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Health Canada, WHO, California) and the 100 µg/L tier (EPA MCL, FDA 21 CFR 165.110) are named and not selected. This cell is published as a FIRM limit rather than as a screen, which is a deliberate departure from the HMTc default for total chromium and is compelled by the instruments themselves: in a food matrix total chromium is dominated by nutritionally benign Cr(III) and is a poor proxy for the health-relevant species, but the drinking-water instruments regulate total chromium precisely because the two species interconvert in aqueous media, and the Health Canada entry states in terms that the maximum acceptable concentration protects against chromium(VI) effects and is established for total chromium. The hexavalent species is not displaced: it is published separately at 10 µg/L.

Cr-VI.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum (California SWRCB Title 22 s.64431 Table 64431-A)
Cr-VI.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Cr-VI.substantiation: Hexavalent chromium at 10 µg/L is the California State Water Resources Control Board Title 22 section 64431 Table 64431-A maximum contaminant level (0.01 mg/L), re-adopted in 2024 after health-risk and feasibility analysis. It is the only enforceable hexavalent-chromium drinking-water maximum set by any government in the register; the sole alternative is the NHMRC guideline that hexavalent chromium should not exceed 50 µg/L, which is named and not selected. California is a sub-national government, so the selection is disclosed as such: it is adopted because it is a binding, enforceable governmental maximum for the same substance in the same basis and because it is the strictest applicable, not because it is federal. HMTc publishes Cr-VI as its own cell in addition to total chromium; a hexavalent result never satisfies the total-chromium cell and a total-chromium result never satisfies this one.

mineral-water.name: Mineral water
mineral-water.native_basis_label: as consumed, per litre of natural mineral water in its packaged state (µg/L; numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
mineral-water.scope_note: In scope: natural mineral water as defined by the recognising authority — water from a protected underground source, bottled at source, of consistent characterising mineral composition, sold without treatment beyond those the instrument permits. This is a legally distinct product form, not a marketing label, and it is the one row of this category where the packaged-water bridge is partly switched off: EU Directive 2020/2184 expressly excludes natural mineral waters recognised under Directive 2009/54/EC from its scope, so no Drinking Water Directive value is used here. The instruments that do reach this form are FDA 21 CFR 165.110 (US law defines mineral water as a type of bottled water at s.165.110(a)(2)(iii), so the standards of quality apply, save that mineral water is exempt from the aesthetically based secondary levels) and the dedicated natural-mineral-water lines of Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, India FSSAI 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Chile Decreto 977/1996 and Fiji FSR 2009. Where those instruments write a product-form split it is preserved rather than smoothed: total chromium is 50 µg/L here against 25 µg/L for other packaged drinking water, and nickel is 20 µg/L here against Hong Kong's 70 µg/L for other packaged drinking water. Out of scope: mineral-fortified or mineralised purified water, which is not natural mineral water and routes to the bottled-drinking-water row or, if flavoured, to Category 5; nothing on the basis of carbonation alone — a naturally carbonated natural mineral water stays on this row.
mineral-water.cross_reference: A naturally carbonated natural mineral water is governed by THIS row, not by the sparkling/carbonated-water row: its legal product form, not its carbonation, determines the applicable instrument. Mineralised or mineral-fortified purified water is not natural mineral water and routes to the bottled-drinking-water row.

mineral-water.basis_guard_note: Every named anchor must be a dietary per-litre / as-consumed water or food-schedule basis. The guard rejects dry-weight, dehydrated, migration/leachate, article material-content and feed bases outright, so a dry-commodity maximum level or a food-contact migration limit can never anchor a per-litre water cell. It admits mg/kg-expressed food-schedule rows (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011) because potable water density is within 0.3 per cent of 1 kg/L, so µg/kg and µg/L are the same number to well inside analytical uncertainty; that is a stated identity, not a silent conversion.

Pb.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum for natural mineral water (FDA 21 CFR 165.110, which covers mineral water as a defined bottled-water type)
Pb.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Pb.substantiation: Lead at 5 µg/L is compelled by FDA 21 CFR 165.110: in US law mineral water is a defined type of bottled water (s.165.110(a)(2)(iii)) and the standards of quality apply to it, so the 0.005 mg/L allowable level is a direct maximum for this product form, not a read-across. It is matched by the Health Canada maximum acceptable concentration and the NHMRC health-based guideline value under the packaged-water bridge. Every mineral-water-specific line in the pool is looser at 10 µg/L (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, India FSSAI 2016, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011) or 50 µg/L (Fiji FSR 2009); all are named and none is selected. The EU Drinking Water Directive value is not used on this row because the Directive excludes natural mineral water from its scope.

Cd.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum (NHMRC Australian Drinking Water Guidelines health-based guideline value)
Cd.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Cd.substantiation: Cadmium at 2 µg/L is the NHMRC Australian Drinking Water Guidelines health-based guideline value (0.002 mg/L), the strictest cadmium maximum any government sets for water. It is applied under the packaged-water bridge stated in the category method note: the product is the same substance in the same per-litre as-consumed basis, and the guideline carries no packaged-product carve-out. The next tier is 3 µg/L (WHO, Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013), then 5 µg/L (EU Drinking Water Directive, FDA 21 CFR 165.110, EPA MCL, California), then 7 µg/L (Health Canada). All are named in the candidate set; none is selected because 2 µg/L is applicable and stricter. The mineral-water-specific lines cluster at 3 µg/L (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, India FSSAI 2016, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011) and are named in the candidate set. Cadmium is a contaminant, not a characterising mineral constituent, so nothing in the natural-mineral-water product definition makes the stricter drinking-water value inapplicable.

tAs.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum for natural mineral water (Hong Kong Cap 132V Part 2 item 2, natural-mineral-waters line)
tAs.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
tAs.substantiation: Total arsenic at 10 µg/L is unanimous across every mineral-water-specific line in the pool (Hong Kong Cap 132V, India FSSAI 2016, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, Israel FCS 2016) and across the packaged-water and drinking-water instruments that reach this form (FDA 21 CFR 165.110, NHMRC, Health Canada, WHO). Only Fiji is looser at 50 µg/L. There is no stricter sovereign total-arsenic value for mineral water anywhere in the register.

iAs.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum for the exact product form (Israel FCS 2016 row 16.1, whose scope names mineral water expressly)
iAs.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
iAs.substantiation: Inorganic arsenic at 6 µg/L is the Israel FCS 2016 maximum level for the exact product form ('Bottled drinking water and mineral water', source row 16.1, 0.006 mg/kg), the strictest sovereign inorganic-arsenic maximum for packaged water in the register. The alternatives are the US EPA drinking-water MCL recorded as inorganic arsenic at 10 µg/L and the Chilean Decreto 977/1996 Article 160 value of 10 µg/L for mineral and packaged drinking waters; both are named and neither is selected because 6 µg/L is applicable and stricter. The species cell is retained separately from total arsenic even though arsenic in potable water is effectively all inorganic, because the HMTc panel never allows a species to satisfy a total: a lot must clear both 10 µg/L total arsenic and 6 µg/L inorganic arsenic. Both named alternatives reach mineral water expressly: the Chilean value covers 'aguas minerales y aguas envasadas para bebida' and the EPA MCL reaches bottled mineral water through the FDA incorporation.

tHg.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum for natural mineral water (Hong Kong Cap 132V Part 2 item 12, natural-mineral-waters line)
tHg.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
tHg.substantiation: Total mercury at 1 µg/L is set for the exact product form by Hong Kong Cap 132V, India FSSAI 2016, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011 and Israel FCS 2016, and is matched by the NHMRC and Health Canada drinking-water values. The looser candidates are FDA 21 CFR 165.110 and Fiji FSR 2009 at 2 µg/L; both are named and neither is selected. Total mercury is published as a total and is never satisfied by a methylmercury or inorganic-mercury result.

not_material.rationale: Mercury in sealed packaged drinking water is present essentially as inorganic Hg(II). The next tier is 3 µg/L (WHO, Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013), then 5 µg/L (EU Drinking Water Directive, FDA 21 CFR 165.110, EPA MCL, California), then 7 µg/L (Health Canada). All are named in the candidate set; none is selected because 2 µg/L is applicable and stricter. CHILD-PROTECTIVE CHECK: the infant-specific cadmium instruments are looser — EU Regulation 2023/915 sets 5 µg/kg for liquid cow-milk-based formula (eu2023_cd_formula_cow_liquid_5), 10 µg/kg for liquid soy-based formula (eu2023_cd_formula_soy_liquid_10) and 20 µg/kg for ready-to-use infant drinks (eu2023_cd_infant_drinks_ready_20); Israel sets 5 µg/kg for ready-to-eat infant and toddler formula. The 2 µg/L drinking-water value is stricter than all of them and is adopted.

tAs.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum; stricter than every infant-specific instrument checked
tAs.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
tAs.substantiation: Total arsenic at 10 µg/L is unanimous across every applicable instrument in the pool: EU Drinking Water Directive, FDA 21 CFR 165.110, the EPA MCL adopted into the bottled-water standard of quality by reference, California, Health Canada, NHMRC, Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011 and the WHO provisional guideline value. There is no stricter sovereign total-arsenic value for water anywhere in the register. Total arsenic is published as its own cell and is not satisfied by the inorganic-arsenic cell. CHILD-PROTECTIVE CHECK: no jurisdiction sets a total-arsenic maximum for infant formula below the drinking-water value. The infant-scoped total-arsenic instruments in the register are India's 50 µg/kg for infant milk substitutes and infant foods (in_tas_infant-milk-substitute-and-infant-foods_50), Singapore's 100 µg/kg for infant formula (sg_foodregs_2026_infant_formula_tas_100) and Israel's 1000 µg/kg for ready-to-eat infant and toddler formula; all are looser than the 10 µg/L value adopted here.

iAs.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum for the exact product form; stricter than every infant-specific instrument checked
iAs.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
iAs.substantiation: Inorganic arsenic at 6 µg/L is the Israel FCS 2016 maximum level for the exact product form ('Bottled drinking water and mineral water', source row 16.1, 0.006 mg/kg), the strictest sovereign inorganic-arsenic maximum for packaged water in the register. The alternatives are the US EPA drinking-water MCL recorded as inorganic arsenic at 10 µg/L and the Chilean Decreto 977/1996 Article 160 value of 10 µg/L for mineral and packaged drinking waters; both are named and neither is selected because 6 µg/L is applicable and stricter. The species cell is retained separately from total arsenic even though arsenic in potable water is effectively all inorganic, because the HMTc panel never allows a species to satisfy a total: a lot must clear both 10 µg/L total arsenic and 6 µg/L inorganic arsenic. CHILD-PROTECTIVE CHECK: EU Regulation 2023/915 sets inorganic arsenic at 10 µg/kg for liquid infant formula (eu2023_ias_formula_liquid_10), Israel at 10 µg/kg for ready-to-eat infant and toddler formula and Brazil at 20 µg/kg for infant formulas. All are looser than the 6 µg/L value adopted here.

tHg.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum; stricter than every infant-specific instrument checked
tHg.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
tHg.substantiation: Total mercury at 1 µg/L is the strictest applicable sovereign maximum, set independently by the EU Drinking Water Directive Annex I Part B, the NHMRC health-based guideline, the Health Canada maximum acceptable concentration (which the source table states applies to all forms of mercury) and the Israel FCS 2016 packaged-water line. The FDA bottled-water allowable level and the California MCL are 2 µg/L and the Vietnamese bottled-water value is 6 µg/L; all are named and none is selected. Total mercury is published as a total and is never satisfied by a methylmercury or inorganic-mercury result. CHILD-PROTECTIVE CHECK: the only infant-specific mercury instrument in the pool is the Israeli value of 4 µg/kg for ready-to-eat infant and toddler formula (il_fcs2016_thg_14_infant_and_toddler_formulas_ready_to_eat_4), four times looser than the 1 µg/L value adopted here.

not_material.rationale: Mercury in sealed packaged drinking water is present essentially as inorganic Hg(II). Methylation is a microbial process requiring anaerobic sulfate- or iron-reducing activity in sediment or biota; it does not occur in a treated, filtered, disinfected and sealed packaged-water matrix, and there is no aquatic food chain in the product to bioaccumulate methylmercury. Methylmercury is in any event a component of total mercury, so it is bounded by identity at the published total-mercury ceiling of 1 µg/L. No separate methylmercury ceiling is published.
not_material.reference_method: Methylmercury is not separately quantified as a routine cell. Total mercury is measured on every certification lot by cold-vapour atomic fluorescence or ICP-MS against the published total-mercury ceiling. Where a lot result reaches or exceeds half the total-mercury ceiling, speciation by GC-ICP-MS or HPLC-ICP-MS is run as a reflex and the source water is investigated; a detectable methyl fraction is an immediate non-conformance regardless of the total-mercury result.
not_material.regulatory_basis: No jurisdiction sets a methylmercury maximum for drinking water, bottled water or natural mineral water. Every drinking-water and packaged-water instrument in the pool regulates mercury as total mercury with no methyl line, and Hong Kong Cap 132V regulates the packaged-drinking-water mercury cell as INORGANIC mercury (0.006 mg/kg, hk_cap132v_ihg_bottled-or-packaged-drinking-waters-other-than-natural_6), which is direct sovereign confirmation that the regulated mercury species in packaged water is the inorganic one. The only methylmercury maxima anywhere in the register are fish and aquatic-animal limits (for example fda_cpg540600_mehg_fish_1000), which govern a bioaccumulating tissue matrix and have no application to water.
not_material.jurisdictions_checked: EU Directive 2020/2184 Annex I; EU Commission Directive 2003/40/EC (natural mineral waters); US EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulations; US FDA 21 CFR 165.110; California SWRCB Title 22 s.64431; Health Canada Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality (2025 summary tables); NHMRC Australian Drinking Water Guidelines; WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality; Hong Kong Cap 132V Part 2; Israel FCS 2016; India FSSAI 2016; Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011; GSO 193/2021; Colombia Res 4506/2013; Chile Decreto 977/1996; Fiji FSR 2009.

Ni.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum; stricter than every infant-specific instrument checked
Ni.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Ni.substantiation: Nickel at 20 µg/L is the EU Drinking Water Directive Annex I Part B parametric value, matched exactly by the NHMRC health-based guideline and by the Hong Kong Cap 132V natural-mineral-waters line. The looser candidates are Hong Kong's 70 µg/L for other packaged drinking waters, the WHO guideline value of 70 µg/L, and 100 µg/L from FDA 21 CFR 165.110 and California; all are named and none is selected. The FDA and California nickel values descend from an EPA nickel MCL that was remanded in 1995, which is a further reason not to treat 100 µg/L as the operative ceiling when a current statutory value of 20 µg/L is applicable. CHILD-PROTECTIVE CHECK: EU Regulation 2024/1987 sets nickel at 100 µg/kg for liquid infant and young-child formula (eu2024_ni_formula_liquid_100), 250 µg/kg for non-soy powder and 400 µg/kg for soy-isolate powder; all are looser than the 20 µg/L value adopted here.

control.rationale: No sovereign sets a tin maximum for drinking water, bottled water or natural mineral water. The drinking-water instrument family carries no tin parameter at all (EU Directive 2020/2184 Annex I Parts B and C; US EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulations; US FDA 21 CFR 165.110 standards of quality; Health Canada; NHMRC; WHO), and none of the national food-schedule packaged-water lines (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, India FSSAI 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Chile Decreto 977/1996, Fiji FSR 2009) carries a tin entry for water. A read-across is not supportable: the nearest sovereign tin maxima are the canned-food and canned-beverage maximum levels, which exist to bound dissolution of tin from a tinplate container wall into an acidic canned matrix, and the canned-beverage value (100 mg/kg inorganic tin) sits roughly four orders of magnitude above anything a packaged water can plausibly contain, so importing it would publish a ceiling that functions as no limit at all. The dominant packaging for this category (PET, HDPE, glass, aluminium) contains no tin. Nursery water is sold in PET or HDPE gallon and litre containers; there is no tinplate presentation of this form. Tin therefore remains a mandatory control cell; no number is invented.
control.reference_method: Tin by ICP-MS on the finished packaged product in its native per-litre as-consumed basis, on every certification lot, reported against the method limit of quantification rather than a ceiling. Any quantifiable tin result triggers investigation of the container, closure and liner, the filling line and the source water, and lot release is withheld pending root-cause identification and a clean re-test. Where the product is presented in a tinplate or tin-coated container, the EU canned-beverage inorganic-tin maximum level recorded as the companion instrument applies as a regulatory hard stop in addition to this control.

Al.label: strictest applicable sovereign value; stricter than every infant-specific instrument checked; an indicator / secondary / aesthetic parameter, disclosed as such
Al.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Al.substantiation: Aluminium at 200 µg/L is the strictest applicable sovereign value and is disclosed here as a non-health-based parameter rather than a toxicological line: it is an Annex I Part C INDICATOR parameter in the EU Drinking Water Directive, a SECONDARY (aesthetically based) allowable level at FDA 21 CFR 165.110, and an AESTHETIC guideline for acid-soluble aluminium in the NHMRC guidelines. The health-based alternatives are far looser (Health Canada's maximum acceptable concentration of 2900 µg/L; California's MCL of 1000 µg/L), so adopting 200 µg/L is the strictest applicable treatment and is materially protective. Its aesthetic derivation is stated rather than concealed because the label of the parameter, not only its number, is part of the provenance. CHILD-PROTECTIVE CHECK: the only infant-specific aluminium maxima in the register are the FSANZ Food Standards Code Schedule 19 values of 500 µg/kg for infant formula and follow-on formula (aunz_sch19_al_formula_nonsoy_500) and 1000 µg/kg for soy-based infant formula (aunz_sch19_al_formula_soy_1000). Both are looser than the 200 µg/L packaged-water parameter adopted here, so the packaged-water value is itself the child-protective one. No infant instrument is adopted and no exposure or occurrence reasoning enters this cell.

Cr.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum; stricter than every infant-specific instrument checked
Cr.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Cr.substantiation: Total chromium at 25 µg/L is the EU Drinking Water Directive Annex I Part B parametric value, the strictest applicable sovereign maximum; it is the Directive's end-state value, to be met by 12 January 2036, with a transitional value of 50 µg/L in force until then. The 50 µg/L tier (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Health Canada, WHO, California) and the 100 µg/L tier (EPA MCL, FDA 21 CFR 165.110) are named and not selected. This cell is published as a FIRM limit rather than as a screen, which is a deliberate departure from the HMTc default for total chromium and is compelled by the instruments themselves: in a food matrix total chromium is dominated by nutritionally benign Cr(III) and is a poor proxy for the health-relevant species, but the drinking-water instruments regulate total chromium precisely because the two species interconvert in aqueous media, and the Health Canada entry states in terms that the maximum acceptable concentration protects against chromium(VI) effects and is established for total chromium. The hexavalent species is not displaced: it is published separately at 10 µg/L. CHILD-PROTECTIVE CHECK: no jurisdiction sets a chromium maximum for infant formula, infant drinks or infant foods below the drinking-water value; the nearest infant-adjacent chromium instrument in the register is China's 2000 µg/kg for milk and modified milk powder (cn_crtotal_milk-powder-and-modified-milk-powder-gen_2000), eighty times looser than the 25 µg/L value adopted here.

Cr-VI.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum; stricter than every infant-specific instrument checked
Cr-VI.basis_label: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Cr-VI.substantiation: Hexavalent chromium at 10 µg/L is the California State Water Resources Control Board Title 22 section 64431 Table 64431-A maximum contaminant level (0.01 mg/L), re-adopted in 2024 after health-risk and feasibility analysis. It is the only enforceable hexavalent-chromium drinking-water maximum set by any government in the register; the sole alternative is the NHMRC guideline that hexavalent chromium should not exceed 50 µg/L, which is named and not selected. California is a sub-national government, so the selection is disclosed as such: it is adopted because it is a binding, enforceable governmental maximum for the same substance in the same basis and because it is the strictest applicable, not because it is federal. HMTc publishes Cr-VI as its own cell in addition to total chromium; a hexavalent result never satisfies the total-chromium cell and a total-chromium result never satisfies this one. CHILD-PROTECTIVE CHECK: no jurisdiction sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum for any infant food or infant beverage. The only stricter hexavalent-chromium values anywhere in the register are the EU Toy Safety Directive migration limits for accessible toy material and for pacifiers and soothers reached via mouthing; those are migration limits on an article, not dietary maxima on an ingested liquid, they are excluded by this row's basis guard, and importing one would be exactly the basis conflation the method forbids.
